academicDiscussion.professorPost: Many towns are reconsidering the names of public landmarks that honor historical figures whose legacies look different under closer scrutiny. In our town, the Whitfield Memorial Bridge still bears the name of a nineteenth-century figure once celebrated as a civic founder, but newly emphasized parts of his record have complicated that reputation. Should the town rename the bridge, or should the original name stay in place? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Priya
studentPosts.post: I think the town should rename the bridge. Once we know a historical figure caused real harm, continuing to honor him with a landmark sends the message that we're comfortable overlooking that harm. Renaming doesn't erase history — it just stops celebrating the parts of it we no longer want to honor.

studentPosts.name: Tomas
studentPosts.post: I disagree with Priya. The bridge's name isn't really about celebrating one person anymore — it's part of how residents give directions and identify their neighborhood. Renaming it risks erasing that everyday connection without actually addressing the harm she's talking about, which deserves its own separate conversation.
